# Data Science Methods

Our analytical work addresses *how* players play, not just output volume. Two models sit on the same 13 per-90 StatsBomb features (attack, progression, defending, efficiency): **PCA + K-Means** for tactical archetypes and **within-context z-score scoring** for club vs national consistency. Both run on a shared automated pipeline (\autoref{fig-architecture}). Full feature definitions, preprocessing steps, and formulas are in the supplementary documentation (\autoref{tbl-appendix-docs}).

## Data Pipeline

StatsBomb open data is ingested through GCS into BigQuery, transformed with dbt (staging, intermediate, marts), enriched by Python ML scripts (`cluster.py`, `consistency.py`), and served through a Django app embedding Looker Studio and a Groq chatbot. Dagster orchestrates weekly full runs and hourly refreshes when new files land in GCS. Deployment and maintenance details are in the supplementary documentation (\autoref{tbl-appendix-docs}).

::: {#fig-architecture fig-pos="H"}

![](../presentation/assets/architecture.png){width=100%}

Automated ELT pipeline: StatsBomb API through BigQuery and dbt to analytics marts, ML outputs, and end-user interfaces.
:::

End-to-end validation confirmed aligned row counts (5,759 player-seasons and 489 dual-context players scored). Mart schemas are documented in the supplementary documentation (\autoref{tbl-appendix-docs}).

## RQ1: Player Archetype Clustering {#sec-rq1-methods}

This section describes the unsupervised clustering model for RQ1. Findings and dashboard outputs are in \hyperref[sec-rq1-results]{RQ1: Role Distribution}.

We cluster player-seasons from `int_player_season_stats` after applying a **270-minute** minimum per season (*n* = 5,469 outfield, 5,759 including goalkeepers). **Goalkeepers** are excluded from K-Means and assigned a fixed label because their event profiles are structurally unlike outfield players.

**Feature selection.** Thirteen per-90 metrics span attacking output (`xg_per_90`, `shots_per_90`), ball progression (`passes_per_90`, `passes_att_third_per_90`, `pass_completion_pct`, `carries_per_90`, `dribbles_per_90`), defensive work (`pressures_per_90`, `interceptions_per_90`, `blocks_per_90`, `clearances_per_90`, `duels_per_90`), and shot efficiency (`xg_per_shot`). The same 13 features are used in clustering, consistency scoring, and the dashboard so labels stay aligned across the product.

**Preprocessing and modelling:** missing values are median-imputed to preserve the zero-skewed shape of defensive counts. Values above the 99th percentile are clipped column-wise to limit outlier influence, then features are standardised. PCA [@jolliffe2016] retains components explaining 80% of variance (typically six). **PC1** captures overall involvement volume. **PC2** contrasts defensive actions against attacking output. K-Means [@lloyd1982] with **k = 5** is applied to the PCA-reduced space. We compared **k = 3–7** using silhouette score; **k = 5** offered the best trade-off between cluster separation and coach-facing interpretability (\hyperref[tbl-appendix-docs]{Notebook 05}). K-Means was preferred over hierarchical methods for scale and reproducibility on 5,000+ player-seasons.

::: {#fig-cluster-scatter fig-pos="H"}

![](../presentation/assets/looker-cluster-scatter-converted.png){width=95%}

Looker cluster explorer scatter plot of player-seasons in PCA space (PC1 vs PC2), coloured by assigned archetype.
:::

The resulting archetypes (\autoref{tbl-cluster-dist}) feed the Looker cluster explorer and chatbot marts. Archetypes describe *how a player is used in a given season*, not a fixed career identity. Lionel Messi is mostly classified as Creative Winger but as Pressing Forward during Copa América 2024, consistent with Argentina's more compact national-team system in that tournament.

Archetype & Seasons & Tactical profile \\

Low Activity & 1,963 & Low volume across all metrics. Typical of squad players and limited roles \\

Creative Playmaker & 807 & High pass completion, progressive passes, carries. Attacking midfielders \\

## RQ2: Club vs National Consistency Scoring {#sec-rq2-methods}

This section describes the within-context scoring model for RQ2. Findings and dashboard outputs are in \hyperref[sec-rq2-results]{RQ2: Club vs National Consistency}.

For **489 dual-context players** with $\geq 270$ minutes in both club and national football, we standardise each of the 13 features **within context**. Club z-scores compare a player only to other club players; national z-scores compare only to national-team peers.

**Z-score standardisation (within each context):**

$$Z = \frac{x - \mu_{\text{context}}}{\sigma_{\text{context}}}$$

**Performance score** (club and national axes on the scatter plot):

$$\text{performance score} = \sum_{i=1}^{13} (Z_i \times w_i)$$

where $Z_i$ is the z-score for per-90 metric $i$ and $w_i$ is its PCA-derived weight (same 13 metrics as RQ1 clustering).

**Consistency score** (profile similarity, not quality level):

$$\text{consistency score} = 1 - \frac{1}{13}\sum_{i=1}^{13} \left|Z_{i,\text{club}} - Z_{i,\text{national}}\right|$$

Quadrants split the cohort at the **medians** of club and national performance score (\autoref{tbl-quadrants}):

| Club vs median | National vs median | Quadrant |
|----------------|-------------------|----------|
| $\geq$ median | $\geq$ median | Elite |
| $\geq$ median | $<$ median | Club Specialist |
| $<$ median | $\geq$ median | International Specialist |
| $<$ median | $<$ median | Underperformer |

: Quadrant assignment logic from `src/ml/consistency.py`. Each quadrant contains roughly one quarter of the cohort. {#tbl-quadrants}

Outputs were sanity-checked against known dual-context players (e.g., Gnabry as International Specialist). Progressive passing into the attacking third best separates club-focused from national-focused specialists in exploratory comparisons. Quadrant labels reflect peer standing within each context, not absolute quality. An Elite player outperforms cohort medians in both settings without any claim about raw output level. The 270-minute threshold removes rotation players, stabilising per-90 estimates at the cost of excluding low-minute prospects relevant to scouting work. Complete formulas and dashboard field definitions are in the supplementary documentation (\autoref{tbl-appendix-docs}).

**Stakeholders and ethics.** Trilemma analysts and partner scouts use archetypes for scouting decisions, and national-team staff use consistency scores for selection. Players are indirectly affected by labels, so outputs are scoped to playing style, not player value. The project is limited to men's senior competitions per StatsBomb open-data coverage and terms of use.

# Data Product and Results

The data product is a unified Django web application combining an embedded Looker Studio dashboard and a natural language chatbot. These forms were chosen because Trilemma's analysts operate at two levels of inquiry that no single tool handles alone: broad visual exploration and specific ad-hoc questions. A notebooks-only approach was ruled out as inaccessible to non-technical partner staff. A dashboard alone could not replace flexible querying without Looker edit access.

## Results

### RQ1: Role Distribution {#sec-rq1-results}

See also \hyperref[sec-rq1-methods]{RQ1: Player Archetype Clustering}. Chi-square tests and Cramér's V on top-five European leagues show **position drives archetype assignment** more strongly than competition (full heatmaps and statistics in \hyperref[tbl-appendix-docs]{Notebook 07}). In row-normalised heatmaps:

- **Center backs** concentrate in Defensive Anchor and Low Activity. Attacking clusters are rare.
- **Forwards and attacking mids** skew toward Pressing Forward and Creative Winger.
- **Central mids** spread across Creative Playmaker, Pressing Forward, and Low Activity, reflecting overlapping box-to-box roles.
- **Full backs** often land in Creative Winger or Creative Playmaker when their profiles emphasise carries and progressive passing.

League effects are secondary but visible (\autoref{tbl-rq1-competition}). Serie A has the largest Low Activity share among the top five. Bundesliga and La Liga show relatively more Pressing Forwards. The same position can shift $\pm 5$–15 percentage points in archetype share between leagues. Dashboard users should filter by position before comparing leagues.

### RQ2: Club vs National Consistency {#sec-rq2-results}

See also \hyperref[sec-rq2-methods]{RQ2: Club vs National Consistency Scoring}. Of 489 dual-context players, **32% are Elite** (above peer median in both contexts), **32% Underperformer**, and **36% single-context specialists** (18% club-only, 18% national-only, see \autoref{tbl-quadrant-dist}). About two thirds of the cohort rank above or below peer median in **both** settings rather than in only one. Comparing Club Specialist vs International Specialist players, the largest gaps are in **passes into the attacking third per 90**, **interceptions per 90**, and **carries into the final third per 90**. System and role differences, not raw goal output, drive the split.

A stable profile is not the same as a strong one. Many players look similar across contexts while ranking below average in both. Defenders show slightly higher mean consistency than forwards (\hyperref[tbl-appendix-docs]{Notebook 08}), suggesting attacking roles shift more between club tactics and national setups. The dashboard's consistency score and context-shift index measure different things (see supplementary documentation, \autoref{tbl-appendix-docs}).

| Quadrant | Players | Share |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Elite | 157 | 32.1% |
| Underperformer | 156 | 31.9% |
| Club Specialist | 88 | 18.0% |
| International Specialist | 88 | 18.0% |

: Observed quadrant counts in `analytics.consistency_scores` (BigQuery). {#tbl-quadrant-dist}

:::

### RQ3: Natural Language Access

The chatbot returns BigQuery-backed answers to plain-English questions in under ten seconds. It was tested manually on representative analyst questions (player rankings by archetype, cross-context comparisons, competition filters) and consistently applied the same eligibility rules as the dashboard, including the 270-minute threshold. Advanced Mode exposes generated SQL for audit. A read-only SQL guard blocks destructive queries.

::: {#fig-chatbot fig-pos="H"}

![](../presentation/assets/chatbot_screenshot.png){width=95%}

:::

## Product Design

The **dashboard** provides visual access to pre-computed results (archetype distributions, consistency quadrants, and player rankings) filterable by position, competition, and archetype without writing code. It is appropriate for regular reporting and for communicating findings to non-technical stakeholders within Trilemma's partner organizations.

The **chatbot** covers ad-hoc questions outside fixed dashboard charts, returning mart-backed answers with SQL audit and read-only guards for trust.

**Strengths:** the Dagster-automated pipeline refreshes all data weekly with zero manual intervention, so both interfaces always reflect current StatsBomb releases. The product is fully reproducible from a single `docker compose up` and documented for independent use by a new team member.

**Limitations:** the chatbot handles single-step queries only — multi-turn reasoning would require session state and prompt chaining beyond the deployment timeline. Both interfaces are scoped to men's competitions; a women's pipeline needs a separate dbt source filter and re-running all intermediate models. Pre-defined dashboard charts cannot be customised without Looker Studio edit access, which was not provisioned for this phase.

# Conclusions and Recommendations

The original problem was that Trilemma Foundation analysts had no scalable way to extract tactical insights from StatsBomb event data without writing complex SQL. This project addressed that problem by delivering three research products on a single automated pipeline.

**RQ1** established that five tactical archetypes emerge from 5,759 player-seasons across 16 competitions, with position being the dominant driver of cluster assignment. Trilemma can now use archetype labels to profile scouting targets and assess squad balance before a transfer window, replacing ad-hoc SQL with a filterable Looker dashboard. **RQ2** found that 36% of dual-context players specialize in one setting (club or national) while 32% perform above peer median in both, providing a data-grounded tool for national team selection decisions. **RQ3** demonstrated that a Groq LLM reliably translates plain English questions into accurate BigQuery SQL, removing the technical barrier for non-technical analysts entirely.

The product addresses the core needs described in the project brief. Remaining limitations are men's-only data scope, uneven StatsBomb open-tier coverage, and the chatbot's single-step reasoning constraint. The models address analytical questions within a defined scope: archetypes profile playing style, not transfer value or injury risk; consistency scores inform national-team context, not squad chemistry or fitness. These boundaries are inherent to the available data, not failures of the models themselves.

Future work should prioritize a women's parallel dbt pipeline branch, multi-turn LLM reasoning with session memory for follow-up questions, integration with the paid StatsBomb API for real-time data, and extending the consistency framework to track how individual archetypes evolve across seasons. A key lesson from the project is that product form matters as much as model quality. Combining a visual dashboard with a conversational interface gives analysts coverage that neither tool provides independently.
